rewrites.58436F8E: Wesgro works on the demand side through six units: Cape Town Air Access, Cruise Cape Town, the Convention Bureau, Destination Marketing, Research and Tourism. Around them sit fifteen external organisations across three tiers of government and industry. Cape Town Air Access is itself a partnership, formed in 2015, of the City of Cape Town, the provincial government, ACSA, Cape Town Tourism, SA Tourism, Wesgro and the private sector. This report is Wesgro's plan and cannot bind the other bodies, so it describes each by its interest and the levers it holds.[^205]
rewrites.2E1B8D4D: The levers that set the pace of growth sit with those partners. National government and its agencies, among them SA Tourism, ACSA and Transnet, hold visa rules, air service agreements, route rights and airport and port operations. The province holds jobs, inclusion and spatial outcomes, sector development, safety programmes and infrastructure planning. The City delivers services, manages precincts and readies events. Industry, from Cape Town Tourism, the V&A Waterfront and the flagship sites to the cruise lines and hotels, holds route viability, demand generation and product standards. Wesgro's plan names energy, ports, rail, digital infrastructure and visas as levers the province influences but does not control. Wesgro has set up an Advocacy and Advisory unit to build the evidence and relationships to influence them.[^206]
rewrites.317902CA: Stakeholders said more about the enabling goal than about either of the others. Of the 223 insights in the engagement record, 91 are coded to this goal: 48 rated High, 38 Medium and 5 Low. Each of the 16 organisations contributed at least one, and Stats SA and the national Department of Tourism spoke to this goal alone. The record's summary condenses the goal into 17 statements under six themes, without ratings. Ratings sit on the organisation rows only and are not defined (Table 2.20).[^208]
rewrites.17D631EE: The summary describes a system short of capacity, money and data. Mandates are fragmented across the three tiers, municipal delivery capacity is uneven and weak or expired partnerships limit implementation. Funding sits below what the growth ambition requires, most of all for destination management, marketing and mobility. The data architecture is too fragmented, lagged and proxy-based to give a reliable provincial view of visitor volumes, spend, spread or economic impact. Community, township and village operators often lack the market readiness, compliance capability and digital skills to reach formal demand channels. Crime perceptions cut across transport, township tourism and international selling; section 2.1 ranks safety among the six barriers. Skills insights sit under other themes.[^210]
rewrites.1380FE11: After a seller, safety is the next gate a visit must pass. Nine of the 20 communities record a safety-perception gap and five record extortion. Seven stakeholder organisations raised safety, and SATVITO reports that negative perceptions of the townships constrain demand for their product. Section 2.1 treats safety perceptions as a barrier to conversion; the concern here is the visit itself. Tourism activity alone cannot resolve crime or extortion. Safety is therefore a launch requirement in its own right, not an outcome of the pilot. No community pilot should open until it is met.[^241]
rewrites.77D2D46A: **Objective 19, Lead removal of infrastructure, visa and safety deficits.** Wesgro works by escalation backed with evidence, because visas and air rights sit nationally. Entry is moving to the Electronic Travel Authorisation, whose performance by nationality is not yet published, and safety and extortion gate activation in up to nine communities. The province's visa study ranks the reforms to press for, and the tourist safety services that already run are the base to build on. Safety perceptions as a barrier to conversion sit in section 2.1.
rewrites.7208A055: Alignment across those tiers is thin. Stakeholders described strain at SA Tourism and a lack of fiscal space. More than twenty bodies produce tourism data, yet the Diagnostic finds no single view of visitor behaviour, which leaves strategy reacting rather than predicting. The Department of Mobility reports the same split in its own field: mobility responsibilities are spread across the three tiers, and local governments often lack the capacity and funding to carry them out.[^207]
rewrites.32ACBFDD: Air rights, the runway and entry rules are held nationally. The Department of Economic Development reports that restrictive bilateral air agreements are limiting airlift growth, leaving the province less competitive than peers. Chinese routes often extend government-to-government relations. The runway that caps peak movements at Cape Town International sits with ACSA, a national body (section 2.4).[^212]
rewrites.3D115EBF: The bodies that manage and sell the destination are weaker than a decade ago. The Department of Economic Development rates Western Cape and Cape Town tourism funding materially below peer destinations for destination management and marketing. It finds that tourism institutional capacity has eroded over the past decade at both provincial and municipal level. It also finds that most local tourism organisations (LTOs) cannot sustain operations without municipal funding.[^215]
rewrites.5E6C9B8D: National Treasury issued MFMA Circular No. 131 on 31 March 2025. It distinguishes an unrequited transfer under section 67 of the Municipal Finance Management Act from a purchase of services, which must follow constitutional procurement and municipal supply-chain rules. In practice it interrupted established municipal funding of LTOs, as the Department of Economic Development finds. Garden Route officials reported in March 2026 that Calitzdorp and Ladismith could not operate fully, that Calitzdorp's office closed from November to February and that Oudtshoorn, De Rust and Plettenberg Bay were affected.
rewrites.7CBB358C: Procurement discipline predates the circular, and partnerships lapse as well as grants. An earlier Auditor-General finding at Mossel Bay recorded tourism spend as irregular where procurement was not followed. Mossel Bay's tourism body still rates its public-private model a structural advantage because it decides faster than a fully municipal one. FEDHASA reports that the memorandum behind the Discover Garden Route partnership has expired and that municipal control over operating terms limited its flexibility.[^217]
rewrites.6491D0D2: Mandates blur at district level. The West Coast District Municipality reports a mandate disconnect between the district, local municipalities and LTOs that leaves tourism development without a clear home. The district moved from a tourism development unit to destination marketing roles, and LTO contracts and budgets are weighted the same way. It asks for tourism development to be written into integrated development plans and spatial frameworks, with reporting.[^218]
rewrites.47327A36: Capital is tightest where the plan needs new sellers. SATVITO reports that access to funding remains a persistent constraint for township and village tourism businesses, and that limited information on support programmes keeps them from help that exists. The committed capital in section 2.4 builds airports, ports, roads, transit and precincts, but none of it funds the bodies that manage and sell the destination. The plan cannot rest on LTOs until their services are contracted on a lawful route and their mandates are settled.[^220]
rewrites.5DE44DCC: Sustainable growth starts with what the destination can carry. Water scarcity limits visitor load in high-growth nodes such as the Garden Route. Boulders is near carrying capacity, and no source yet measures the carrying capacity of any flagship (section 2.4). Climate adds a dated cost. Robben Island Museum loses about R16 million a year to weather-cancelled trips, and CapeNature reports climate-related flooding, fire and heat closing sites. CapeNature also finds off-grid solar and self-sufficiency increasingly necessary to keep remote sites in service. Sustainable destination management is risk management for the province's flagship product today, and should be funded as such, not as a later add-on.[^221]
rewrites.6004A39B: The data holders describe what the public series can show. Stats SA publishes monthly international tourism data with a lag of about one month, covering traveller volumes, trip purpose, mode of transport and regional distribution. Its domestic tourism survey draws on a large household sample, and Stats SA is raising its household sample from 30,000 to 40,000 while it tests a continuous population survey. It is also developing safety and security data for analysis at municipal level.[^223]
rewrites.348EF2FE: The national Department of Tourism sets out what those series cannot show. Border-arrival data gives no spend, length of stay or provincial spread, which depend on SA Tourism's departure survey. Airport passenger and credit card data include non-tourists and can overstate visitor volumes or spend unless filtered. Stats SA and SA Tourism survey domestic tourism by different methods and produce inconsistent figures.[^224]
rewrites.58EF9D92: Below the national series, operators and local bodies work from proxies. Mossel Bay's tourism body compiles demand from several proxies for want of one funded platform. C-BRTA collects passenger lists from cross-border operators that are never turned into source-market or visitor-flow analysis. Robben Island Museum cannot link marketing spend to visitors gained. Google reports that market-level search data can show which overseas markets already take an interest in the Western Cape, but data specific to the province is not confirmed as available.[^225]
rewrites.62A2F41F: The forums serve marketing better than development. The West Coast District Municipality reports that provincial and regional forums are dominated by destination marketing, and that provincial support, Wesgro's strategy and district needs are poorly matched on grants, capacity building and skills. Where the task is selling, collaboration is reported to work: the CTICC describes effective joint bidding, and !Khwa ttu markets itself through LTOs, community partners and content creators.[^227]
rewrites.4195F5A5: Policy settings lag the task in several places. The Department of Economic Development reports a provincial policy gap: legislation is limited and earlier policy and master-planning frameworks are out of date. At !Khwa ttu, transport cost keeps public schools away, and curriculum-linked visits at scale would need support from the Education Department or another public mechanism. Circular 131 is a further case (see Funding and mandates above).[^228]
rewrites.683D387C: Stakeholders place safety inside transport. The Department of Mobility reports that safety concerns in public transport make shared options less attractive to visitors. C-BRTA reports taxi-operator extortion at border posts, where passengers are forced off vehicles and cash is demanded before a trip continues.[^230]
rewrites.38BBFFEC: Reliable measures of tourism's jobs, its contribution to GDP and small-business participation are work for execution. The national Department of Tourism reports no approved official methodology for provincial tourism GDP and jobs estimates. A named workstream in I16, Tourism economic measures, builds one, fed by the labour analysis in I18. Stats SA cites 749 vacancies behind delays to the tourism satellite account and infers provincial flows partly from ports-of-entry data.[^231]
rewrites.121AF459: Stakeholders describe the same gap from the seller's side. SATVITO reports that many township and village businesses lack market readiness, from compliance to an understanding of buyers, and so cannot reach trade platforms or incentive programmes. The Overberg District finds that established capital has driven tourism development and that community products need sustained mentoring. The West Coast District Municipality reports no medium-term approach behind township tourism.[^240]
rewrites.2476C2F4: Inclusion here means activity inside the community. A tour, a meal, a bed or a market counts; a resident commuting to a hotel job in town does not. Inclusion turns on where visitor spend lands, not on how many visitors come.[^236]
rewrites.2E3FC835: Community supply is not one thing. It includes owner-run enterprises as well as collective projects, so a place called community tourism does not establish collective ownership. Each candidate needs an operator and rights register before it is promoted.
rewrites.2D1912B0: The first output is deliberately small: one live booking route, published operating dates, a named customer contact and a simple record of bookings and local revenue. Most first moves carry no dedicated budget line. Chapter 4 sets out roles and funding. The order the cases support (section 2.2) becomes the order of delivery: a seller first, then a safe visit, then product and exposure.[^245]
rewrites.09C85381: Two plans reach into the visitor's trip. The Department of Mobility's draft Provincial Land Transport Framework includes a Tourism Transport Strategy, which plans to revive the MyCiTi airport service with ACSA and to sign and maintain tourist routes. The City's framework for 2019 to 2024 set out a Tourist Safety Programme of secure zones in higher-risk tourism areas, a Tourist Police unit, victim support and safety forums, and parts of it now run. The action plan should build on both rather than start new ones. Which parts of the department's Tourism Transport Strategy are adopted, funded or running is not confirmed.[^229]
rewrites.30A8ED31: Remote communities with underused assets, 7 long-listed and 2 shortlisted, need access opened and the asset placed on a route product the LTO already sells. Atlantis is classed remote by Wesgro's naming, though it lies 26 minutes from Darling. Remote communities with nothing inside, 8 long-listed and 1 shortlisted, need procurement and skills first and an asset only once a route product exists. The first move differs by type, but in each the seller or the route comes before the asset.[^243]
rewrites.7467392F: Rail and regional buses are closer to use than to a visitor product. The Southern Line runs from Cape Town to Fish Hoek, with a Simon's Town section whose regular service PRASA has yet to confirm. Trains do not normally run on Sundays or public holidays, and Boulders needs a transfer from Simon's Town station. The City's rail business plan favours transferred services with private operating participation, and the National Rail Master Plan went to consultation in April 2026; neither is an executed devolution.

inserts.text: The circular does not prohibit funding tourism organisations: the contracted-services route remains open, and the City of Cape Town processed its first Cape Town Tourism payment that way (City mid-year report, January 2026). The scale is not known: no source counts the organisations affected or their funding before and after, George's integrated tourism unit was unaffected and the Garden Route reports are attributed statements, not an audited inventory.[^216]

GO GEORGE requires its own R45 smart card, which can be loaded with cash, a debit or credit card or a SASSA card, and its single fare from July 2026 is R18.50. What is unresolved is tapping a bank card directly on the bus, which national integrated-fare regulations already contemplate. GO GEORGE trialled an airport service in September 2026.
